failure_reason: No contention was actually created. The long_tx likely did not hold exclusive row locks on hot TPCC keys (e.g., it used plain SELECTs or updated non-hot keys), and there was little or no conflicting traffic hitting the same rows. As a result, Innodb_row_lock_time and Innodb_row_lock_waits did not increase, no statements crossed the slow-query threshold, and overall QPS did not drop. Additionally, the lock hold time was probably shorter than the typical slow-log threshold (10s), so even if there were waits they weren’t recorded as slow queries. If only long_tx was injected, the chain cannot propagate without a conflicting writer swarm targeting the same rows.
suggested_changes: Make long_tx hold real X locks on hot TPCC rows for >30–60s. Use UPDATE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a small, fixed hot key set (e.g., warehouse w_id=1, district w_id=1,d_id=1, and one customer row) and hold the transaction with DO SLEEP(60) before COMMIT. This directly drives Innodb_row_lock_time up.

Align conflict traffic exactly to those locked rows. Ensure your contention generator continuously executes short UPDATEs against the same hot key (e.g., UPDATE district SET d_ytd = d_ytd + 1 WHERE w_id=1 AND d_id=1) with high concurrency (32–64 sessions) and no think time. This drives Innodb_row_lock_waits up and creates blocked sessions.

Increase wait durations to exceed slow-query threshold. Either set session long_query_time=1 for the conflictors or ensure the lock hold time is >12–15s so blocked statements are logged as slow. Also set session innodb_lock_wait_timeout >= hold time (e.g., 120s) so they wait rather than time out.

Order the actions: start long_tx first, confirm it acquired locks, then start the contention storm 1–2s later, and run for ≥90–120s so ratio-based metrics (Innodb_row_lock_time/waits) and slow_query_count have time to show ≥2× increases.

If you only injected long_tx and did not inject any conflicting writer workload, you need to add a lock-contention generator targeting the same keys; otherwise the chain long_tx -> lock_contention -> slow_query -> qps_drop cannot be reproduced.

If TPCC background load is present and configurable, pin it to the same warehouse (e.g., W_ID=1) during the experiment window to amplify contention. Otherwise rely on the explicit contention generator to provide the required waits.
Monitor for blocked_session_count during the run; if it stays near zero, your conflict SQL is not hitting the same rows as long_tx. Adjust predicates until blocked sessions rise.

transaction_script_steps: UPDATE warehouse SET w_ytd = w_ytd WHERE w_id = 1
UPDATE district SET d_ytd = d_ytd WHERE w_id = 1 AND d_id = 1
SELECT c_balance FROM customer WHERE w_id = 1 AND d_id = 1 AND c_id = 1 FOR UPDATE
/* loop this block continuously for the duration */
UPDATE district SET d_ytd = d_ytd + 1 WHERE w_id = 1 AND d_id = 1

risk_warning: These changes will intentionally create heavy lock contention and long waits. Expect deadlocks and lock wait timeouts, large undo/history growth, replication lag or binlog spikes, thread pool saturation, and potential connection pile-up. Run only in an isolated test environment, set innodb_lock_wait_timeout sufficiently high to avoid premature timeouts, and monitor disk space for undo/binlog growth. Ensure you stop the contention storm before saturating the instance.
